page: The Microsoft Azure E64-16as_v7 is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance based on the AMD EPYC 9V45 processor, running under the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is allocated 16 dedicated vCPUs spanning 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled at clock speeds up to 4.5 GHz. Each physical core features 48 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and access to 32 MB of shared L3 cache. It incorporates vector instruction extensions including AVX-512 and cryptographic accelerators such as AES and SHA-NI.

A defining characteristic of this configuration is its high memory-to-vCPU allocation. The instance is provisioned with 512.0 GB of system memory, yielding 32.0 GB per virtual processor. In memory tests, it achieved a strong PassMark memory score of 2774.04, supported by uncached read bandwidth of 51.28 GB/s and write bandwidth of 34.22 GB/s. The instance provides no bundled local storage, requiring network-attached remote block volumes such as Azure Premium Storage for persistent file and database operations. No hardware accelerators or GPUs are included.

Benchmark outcomes demonstrate top-tier single-core execution speed, driven by the 4.5 GHz AMD Zen architecture. The instance achieved top-decile ratings in single-threaded stress-ng tests, gzip compression at 41.43 GB/s, and bzip3 single-threaded decompression at 18.43 GB/s. Because total execution is limited to 16 vCPUs constrained within a 64-vCPU-scale chassis, multi-threaded CPU throughput registers in the middle tier across PassMark and stress-ng suites. In caching and key-value environments, the instance sustained 27.35 million Redis SET operations per second.

The architecture of the E64-16as_v7 provides distinct cost efficiency for workloads constrained by memory capacity rather than core counts. Deployments that require vast memory allocations without incurring licensing or provisioning overhead for unneeded CPU cores benefit from this constrained vCPU design. Appropriate workloads include enterprise in-memory caches, memory-resident analytics, transactional database systems, and small-model inference tasks.
